clinician.trajectory_summary: A 40-year-old female presented with an 18-month history of an intermittently painful mass in the medial aspect of her right forearm, which became increasingly tender and firm before and during menstruation. Physical examination revealed a small palpable mass in the right flexor pronator musculature, tender to palpation. Initial imaging included an ultrasound, which showed a circumscribed and hypoechoic mass with internal Doppler flow. An MRI without intravenous contrast further characterized the mass as an oval intramuscular mass (2.2 × 2.1 × 3.0 cm) in the anterior compartment of the proximal forearm, demonstrating heterogeneous T2 signal and cystic changes, with no invasion. After a non-diagnostic core needle biopsy, an open biopsy with frozen section diagnosis was performed, which was consistent with endometriosis. Following diagnosis, the patient was referred to Obstetrics/Gynecology. Additional history revealed three uncomplicated Cesarean sections, and there was no concern for pelvic endometriosis. Approximately 18 months after initial presentation, the patient's symptoms worsened, with pain radiating into the elbow, distal forearm, and hand.
